NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K warns that customers' and partners' ability to secure capital and energy to build complex datacenter infrastructure is among the key demand drivers, noting that "Expanding energy capacity to meet demand is a complex, multi-year process involving significant regulatory, technical, and construction challenges [1]." AMD's FY2025 10-K states that demand for its AI accelerators depends on the extent to which customers utilize generative AI solutions and that "both the near-term and long-term trajectory of such generative AI solutions is unknown," adding that some customers "may be unable to secure access to internal and external infrastructure, including availability of sufficient data center capacity or energy for the buildout of data centers that use our products [2]." Intel's FY2025 10-K warns that its investments to address AI demand "may be insufficient" and that it faces significant hurdles "including whether demand will materialize" and whether it can develop products competitive with more established offerings and ecosystems [3].

On the supply side, NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K states that it has previously experienced extended lead times of "more than 12 months" and has "paid premiums, provided deposits, and entered into long-term supply agreements and capacity commitments" to secure future capacity [4]. NVIDIA also warns that more frequent architecture transitions and a larger number of product configurations "may magnify the challenges associated with managing our supply and demand which may further create volatility in our revenue," with customers potentially delaying adoption if their data center infrastructure is not ready [5]. Intel's FY2025 10-K, by contrast, describes having "missed the significant shift in compute demand to GPUs optimized for AI workloads" and recognized "Gaudi AI accelerator inventory-related charges of $375 million in 2025 and $922 million in 2024" from its unsuccessful efforts to compete in the accelerator market [6].

Microsoft's FY2026 10-K states that "Demand for cloud-based and AI products and services is evolving and difficult to forecast," cautioning that overestimation of demand "may result in underutilization of infrastructure and may lead to impairment of assets on our balance sheet," while demand exceeding available capacity limits its ability to meet customer needs in a timely manner [7]. Microsoft further identifies the cost structure for AI products and services as subject to "significant uncertainty, including with respect to model training and inference costs, the availability and pricing of components, and energy costs [7]." Meta's FY2025 10-K notes that its ability to develop and deploy AI technologies "is dependent on access to specific third-party equipment, technology, and other technical and physical infrastructure...as to which we cannot control the availability or pricing, especially in a highly competitive environment [8]." Alphabet's FY2025 10-K warns that significant leasing arrangements and "large, long-duration commercial agreements" for AI compute capacity increase liabilities and that in nonperformance or an industry downturn the company "may incur additional liabilities, have excess capacity that we cannot easily redeploy, and not receive payments from our counterparties or customers [9]."

Alphabet's FY2025 10-K identifies that "manufacturing and supply of servers and network equipment for our technical infrastructure, particularly for specialized AI chips, is limited to a small number of qualified suppliers," while also noting that "energy supply is constrained globally due to the significant increase in demand for and limited availability of energy to power AI compute [10]." Amazon's FY2025 10-K warns that it relies on "a limited group of suppliers for semiconductor products, including products related to artificial intelligence infrastructure such as graphics processing units," and that "Constraints on the availability of these products could adversely affect our ability to develop and operate artificial intelligence technologies, products, or services [11]." Microsoft's FY2026 10-K notes that it has experienced and may continue to experience "supply constraints, including shortages of semiconductors, networking equipment, power systems, cooling equipment, and other key components," and that expanding manufacturing or supply capacity for certain components "may require significant investments and multi-year lead times [12]."
